item.title: Hydraulic cranes of Laodicea
item.description: But one of the first things we see as we walk here today is a giant hydraulic crane raising and positioning huge blocks of ancient stone. Sending one of those babies back in time would be an untold blessing to the ancient builders, I can’t help thinking.

item.title: Wreck of faith in Philadelphia
item.description: There’s not much left of Philadelphia, despite it having the most modern-sounding name of all the seven churches of the Apocalypse. All that remains is a piece of ground the size of a postage stamp, and on it the noble wreck of a gigantic church.

item.title: Demons and crosses in Sardis
item.description: The place here which seized my imagination was the ruined Temple of Artemis, which is in a remote field outside town, overlooked by curious hills shaped like pointed hoods. The place is lonely, melancholy and haunted – and maybe a bit dark too.

item.description: A wonder on every corner of Ephesus

item.title: Heaven open on Holy Patmos
item.description: High over the town on a hill is the Monastery of St John the Theologian. Late morning a taxi bore us up to the Cave of the Apocalypse, below the monastery.

item.title: Bring Up the Bodies
item.description: A new book came out yesterday... except, hang on, it isn’t new. Publisher Fourth Estate has released the paperback edition of Bring Up the Bodies a full year after the hardback publication, and seven months since Hilary Mantel won the Man Booker.

item.title: Remembering our dog Sasha
item.description: She and I walked every weekday in the big spaces of Gunnersbury Park. Her habitual sin was hanging back. She hung back in her endless quest for food. She was one-third Labrador, you see, even though she looked like a large fox.

item.title: Lives of the coin-operated saints
item.description: I’ve never seen a saint bashing herself in the face with a pair of pincers before. But as I entered Michael Landy’s Saints Alive exhibition at the National Gallery this morning, there guarding the way in was a 3 metre tall St Apollonia, in a floor-length red dress.

item.title: A Vicar, Crucified
item.description: Simon Parke’s absorbing murder mystery novel "A Vicar, Crucified" has more twists than a hangman’s noose and is written by a former vicar who has the inside story on the many reasons why parishioners might reasonably want to murder their priest.

item.title: I took the ‘Which animal dropping are you?’ quiz and got ‘Elephant poo’
item.description: I took the 'Which animal dropping are you?' quiz on Facebook and got 'Elephant poo'.
